newsitem.title: USA: Stock selloff undermines investors confidence.
newsitem.headline: Stock selloff undermines investors confidence.

text.p: Back-to-back weekly retreats in Wall Street stocks have undermined investor confidence but analysts are reluctant to declare the bull market dead.
Most of last week's damage occured on Friday, a day of double-witching expirations of individual stock options and stock index options.

"It's always difficult on one of these expiration days to be sure what you have, especially a Friday in August when markets are thinner and the action is more erratic," said Eric Miller, strategist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette Securities Corp.
The Dow's slumped 247.37 points to 7,695.66 Friday -- its second-biggest point loss ever -- and erased 337 points from the blue-chip index for the week. In the prior week the Dow fell 163 points.
There was no single reason analysts could point to as being responsible for the end-of-week plunge, but a number of disparate events seemed to have unnerved investors and clouded the outlook.
Miller said that AMG Data Services said on Friday that a net $827 million flowed out of equity mutual funds in the week ended Aug. 13. It was the first weekly outflow since April.
"The fact that maybe the market did not behave in logical fashion has unnerved people just a little," said Miller.
One of the anomalies to ponder was the fact that the retreat in stocks occurred while bonds remained steady.

In recent years, bonds and stocks have move in lockstep, with the lower yields that accompany higher bond prices seen as an inducement to buy stocks and vice versa. The yield on the long Treasury issues was 6.55 percent, little changed on the week.

Noting the strength in bonds, Trude Latimer, an independent analyst based in Charlottesville, Va., suggested that rather than trying to lock in a return investors were looking for something that resembled a safe haven.
"I think there has been a deterioration in the stock market in the last three to four weeks," Latimer said.

Also puzzling was the background of economic news last week which was generally viewed as positive for stocks and bonds. In one set of reports on Wednesday wholesale prices fell 0.1 percent in July for a record seventh straight month, while retail sales rose 0.6 percent.
"The thing to watch will be Monday morning," said Ken Tower, technical analyst at UST Securities Corp. "If you have a strong day on Monday you pretty well discount what was going on Friday."
Miller believes that the stock market was "just vulnerable to some loss of confidence."
He said it will now face a period of "indigestion" but "I don't think we're due for a signficant decline."

Tower said he misjudged the latest move and was expecting another pop higher in the 8,200-8,300 area for the Dow before a correction amounting to 5 to 10 percent. Friday's pullback left the market down 6.8 percent from the all-time high of 8,259.31 reached Aug. 6.

One culprit in Friday's drop was an earnings warning from Gillette Co., which late Thursday suggested that its earnings for 1997 would be in the lower end of a range of $2.55 to $2.60 per share. Gillette fell 4-3/16 to 85-7/8 Friday.
Exactly one week earlier, Coca-Cola Co said its third-quarter earnings would be only "slightly higher" than a year ago. That sparked a selloff in the company's shares.

Coke's and Gillette's problems have been cited as factors in a rotation of stock investments away from defensive stable-demand consumer issues and into cyclicals such as metals, forest products and autos.

"Gillette's earnings warning, fairly soon after that of Coca-Cola, has dented blue chip mystique a little bit," Miller said. But overall, he thinks earnings for the third quarter ending in September "should still be pretty good."
Friday's rout on Wall Street followed a 2.43 percent decline that day in Hong Kong, the biggest for that market in two months, and a 2.5 percent decline in the FTSE-100 blue chip index in London.

Analysts said there was not necessarily any direct connection to Friday's retreat on Wall Street. As a rule, one said, foreign markets react to Wall Street rather than the other way around. Hong Kong will be closed Monday for a holiday.
